content_voiceover: This graph captures the modern, cell-based model of coagulation as a curve of thrombin generation over time, divided into three phases. The first phase, initiation, happens on tissue-factor-bearing cells at the site of injury, where small amounts of thrombin are generated, just enough to prime the system, and the curve stays essentially flat here. The second phase, propagation, is where the curve rises steeply, this is when platelets have been activated and provide the phospholipid surface for the tenase and prothrombinase complexes to assemble at high density, producing an explosive burst of thrombin generation, sometimes called the thrombin burst. This burst is what generates enough thrombin to convert fibrinogen to fibrin rapidly and to activate factor XIII for cross-linking. The third phase, termination, is where natural anticoagulant mechanisms, like antithrombin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, and the protein C system, rein in the process, and thrombin generation plateaus, keeping the clot localized and preventing runaway systemic coagulation. Understanding this cell-based, three-phase model helps explain clinical bleeding and clotting disorders far better than the classic intrinsic-extrinsic cascade alone, and it's increasingly emphasized on hematology boards.
keypoints: Initiation: small thrombin generation on tissue-factor-bearing cells
Propagation: explosive thrombin burst on activated platelet surfaces
Termination: natural anticoagulants plateau thrombin generation
The cell-based model better explains real-world bleeding and clotting than the classic cascade
keypoint_voiceover: Three phases to remember. Initiation is slow and localized, propagation is the thrombin burst on platelets, and termination is where antithrombin and protein C shut the process down.
